\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

All eight generators are base (pretrained) models.
This is a deliberate design choice: base models isolate the generation mechanism from instruction-tuning effects, enabling controlled study of recursive distributional drift.
However, web text is predominantly produced by instruction-tuned and RLHF-aligned models.
Preliminary instruct experiments confirm that depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning: OLMo-2-1B-Instruct drops to within-model 3-class F1\,=\,0.575 (vs.\ 0.754 base) and Llama-3.2-3B to 0.544 (vs.\ 0.742 base; Table~\ref{tab:instruct}).
Length-matched analysis yields near-zero correlations ($|\rho| < 0.02$) and binary classification near chance (F1\,$\approx$\,0.5) for Qwen models, leaving interpretation ambiguous.
Extending depth fingerprinting to instruct models requires addressing these confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping) that instruction tuning introduces.

Our experiments include generators up to 8.2B parameters (Qwen3-8B).
Depth signal persists at this scale (Qwen3-8B 3-class F1\,=\,0.714), but cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap vs.\ $\leq$2.8B generators (F1\,=\,0.77--0.81).
Gemma-2-2B shows the weakest generalization among nine generators (3-class F1\,=\,0.628), with gen-1 nearly indistinguishable from other classes (per-class F1\,=\,0.036); this architecture-specific limitation is discussed in Appendix~\ref{app:9gen-scale}.
Frontier models (70B+) remain untested; their higher fluency may further compress feature margins.

Differential depth response strength is prompt-type dependent: within-type 3-class F1 ranges from 0.78 (continuation) to 0.73 (elaboration), with inspired rewriting intermediate at 0.74 (Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}).
DDR is most reliably detected in continuation-style generation; near-paraphrastic settings approach the method's detection floor.
Cross-prompt-type transfer (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753) confirms shared signal, yet additional prompt types (e.g., summarization, instruction following) and cross-generator $\times$ cross-prompt interactions remain untested.

Our primary evaluation uses single-generator chains; cross-model chains (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}) confirm depth signal under generator heterogeneity (3-class F1\,=\,0.789, binary F1\,=\,0.830; evaluated on the 5-generator subset for which cross-model chains were available), though these generators represent a controlled laboratory setting rather than the full diversity of real-world contamination.
Simulated human editing (\S\ref{sec:discussion}) suggests graceful degradation, but the gap between simulated token replacement and real-world post-processing remains untested.
Independent gen-0 seed sets per generator would eliminate potential memorization effects in 3-class LOGO evaluation; we report leak-free binary F1 as the primary metric to mitigate this limitation.

The reference model is fixed to Pythia-410M throughout, although cross-family reference experiments (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) confirm the phenomenon is not reference-specific (spread 0.013 across three references).
All seed texts in the main evaluation are English Wikipedia excerpts.
Cross-domain evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:domain}) shows that depth signal persists across News, Academic, and Code domains (binary F1 $>$ 0.73 under LOGO at $t{=}1.0$), though a domain $\times$ temperature interaction exists: certain domain/generator combinations at lower temperature approach chance level (e.g., Academic domain binary F1\,=\,0.628 at $t{=}0.7$), suggesting that reference model calibration is critical for cross-domain deployment.
The reference model dependency (Pythia-410M, English-centric pretraining) limits non-English applicability and adds inference overhead relative to surface-feature-only approaches.
Generalization to other languages remains untested.

Our default analysis uses fixed decoding parameters (temperature 0.7, nucleus $p{=}0.9$). A sampling ablation (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}) shows robustness to moderate variation ($t \in [0.5, 0.7]$, ${\leq}0.3$\,pp) but substantial degradation at $t{=}1.0$ ($-6$\,pp), indicating that depth fingerprinting assumes standard decoding regimes.
Cross-temperature transfer shows substantial degradation when test-time temperature exceeds training-time settings, limiting deployment to scenarios where the generation temperature is approximately known.

We use 3-class granularity (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+). A 5-class evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}) yields LOGO F1\,$\approx$\,0.50, with depths 2--4 mutually indistinguishable, validating the 3-class design as the practical resolution limit.

\label{sec:discussion}

Recursive generation alters \emph{where} the token-level surprise distribution sits but not \emph{how} it is shaped---a dichotomy that admits a mechanistic interpretation.
Under nucleus sampling, top-$p$ truncation selects from a fixed probability-mass fraction at each step, preserving the functional form of the conditional distribution regardless of input content.
What changes across recursive steps is the \emph{input} to this truncation: as the model conditions on its own increasingly self-typical outputs, the expected token-level NLL compresses monotonically---each generation feeds slightly more predictable input into the same shape-preserving mechanism.
This account yields two testable predictions: (1)~increasing sampling randomness should weaken the location drift by disrupting mode-seeking, and (2)~semantic-preservation constraints should attenuate it by anchoring the input distribution.
Both are empirically confirmed: at $t{=}1.0$, the location signal collapses ($\rho$: $-0.60 \to -0.002$; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}); under elaboration prompts, drift weakens relative to continuation (F1\,=\,0.730 vs.\ 0.781; Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}), consistent with \citet{broken_telephone}, while cross-type transfer remains viable (F1\,=\,0.753).
Permutation importance, Granger causality, and feature intervention analyses provide further causal evidence: drifting features contribute $5.5\times$ more to classification than near-stationary ones, with 6/7 features exhibiting significant Granger causality (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-causality}).

The classifier is a proof-of-concept, not a deployable system: document-level gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.63 and ${\sim}30\%$ error rate are insufficient for automated filtering but sufficient for corpus-level auditing ($O(1/\sqrt{n})$ error scaling), with the primary difficulty being gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ discrimination (86\% false negatives; Appendix~\ref{app:error-analysis}).
Concretely, in a training-data curation pipeline, the classifier can estimate the proportion of recursively generated text in a candidate corpus: at $n{=}1{,}000$ documents, the gen-2+ fraction estimate has ${\sim}$$\pm$3--4\% margin under LOGO conditions, sufficient to flag batches exceeding a contamination threshold (e.g., $>$10\% gen-2+) for further review or exclusion.
This batch-level application sidesteps the per-document error rate that limits individual flagging.
Detection thus serves not only as a provenance signal but also as a prophylactic against model collapse: \citet{drayson_detection_prevents_collapse} show that filtering synthetic content from training corpora preserves model quality across iterative retraining cycles.
In generator-unknown deployment, LOGO F1\,=\,0.694 provides a conservative lower bound (9.1\,pp per-generator spread); cross-temperature transfer degrades when test-time temperature exceeds training (F1\,$\to$\,0.723; Appendix~\ref{app:cross-temp}).

Preliminary evidence from a 14.7B generator (Qwen3-14B-Base) confirms that the DDR partition persists at larger scale: Cohen's $d$ for drifting features remains in the large-effect range ($d{=}0.78$--$1.12$), though Spearman $|\rho|$ attenuates by 21--35\%, with entropy mean falling just below the drifting threshold ($|\rho|{=}0.39 < 0.40$, $d{=}0.78$).
This scale-dependent signal compression is consistent with larger models producing more self-typical outputs that narrow inter-depth contrasts; the partition structure is preserved even as absolute effect sizes compress.

DDR connects to but is mechanistically distinct from model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse}: retraining permanently erodes tail coverage by updating model weights, whereas inference-chain drift at fixed parameters shifts only the NLL distribution's location, leaving its shape as a stable reference.
Crucially, vocabulary impoverishment alone cannot explain DDR: if depth merely simplified the lexicon, shape features should also compress, yet entropy extremes and tail decay remain stable across all eight generators ($d < 0.10$; \S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
Moreover, semantic similarity between adjacent depths \emph{increases} monotonically (cosine: 0.62$\to$0.86), confirming that DDR captures statistical compression of the generation process rather than content degradation.
Prior work documents \emph{what converges}---diversity loss \cite{curious_decline}, attractor dynamics \cite{markovian_chains}, mode collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion}---but not what is \emph{preserved}; this complementary observation is what enables depth detection without per-generator calibration.
Three depth classes represent the practical resolution ceiling (5-class F1\,$\approx$\,0.50; Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}), though QLoRA recovers substantially more signal (F1\,=\,0.905; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}); the $+$11.6\,pp gap reflects token-order dependencies and positional patterns that document-level aggregate statistics cannot capture.
Instruction-tuned models show attenuated fingerprints (OLMo-Instruct 3-class F1\,=\,0.575 vs.\ 0.754 base; DDR silhouette compresses from 0.632 to 0.338) with reversed feature correlations: alignment does not fully eliminate the depth signal, though it compresses the feature-space structure that enables cross-generator detection.
This interpretation is supported by QLoRA's recovery to 0.89--0.91 on instruct data (Appendix~\ref{app:instruct}), confirming that the signal persists at the token-sequence level even when aggregate features lose discriminative power.
The base-model restriction thus reflects both degraded DDR structure (compressed partition) and feature-set limitations; the token-level signal that QLoRA exploits may draw on representational patterns beyond DDR's location/shape decomposition, a hypothesis testable in future work.

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

All eight generators are base (pretrained) models.
This is a deliberate design choice: base models isolate the generation mechanism from instruction-tuning effects, enabling controlled study of recursive distributional drift.
However, web text is predominantly produced by instruction-tuned and RLHF-aligned models.
Preliminary instruct experiments confirm that depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning: OLMo-2-1B-Instruct drops to within-model 3-class F1\,=\,0.575 (vs.\ 0.754 base) and Llama-3.2-3B to 0.544 (vs.\ 0.742 base; Table~\ref{tab:instruct}).
Length-matched analysis yields near-zero correlations ($|\rho| < 0.02$) and binary classification near chance (F1\,$\approx$\,0.5) for Qwen models, leaving interpretation ambiguous.
Extending depth fingerprinting to instruct models requires addressing these confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping) that instruction tuning introduces.

Our experiments include generators up to 8.2B parameters (Qwen3-8B).
Depth signal persists at this scale (Qwen3-8B 3-class F1\,=\,0.714), but cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap vs.\ $\leq$2.8B generators (F1\,=\,0.77--0.81).
Gemma-2-2B shows the weakest generalization among nine generators (3-class F1\,=\,0.628), with gen-1 nearly indistinguishable from other classes (per-class F1\,=\,0.036); this architecture-specific limitation is discussed in Appendix~\ref{app:9gen-scale}.
Frontier models (70B+) remain untested; their higher fluency may further compress feature margins.

Differential depth response strength is prompt-type dependent: within-type 3-class F1 ranges from 0.78 (continuation) to 0.73 (elaboration), with inspired rewriting intermediate at 0.74 (Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}).
DDR is most reliably detected in continuation-style generation; near-paraphrastic settings approach the method's detection floor.
Cross-prompt-type transfer (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753) confirms shared signal, yet additional prompt types (e.g., summarization, instruction following) and cross-generator $\times$ cross-prompt interactions remain untested.

Our primary evaluation uses single-generator chains; cross-model chains (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}) confirm depth signal under generator heterogeneity (3-class F1\,=\,0.789, binary F1\,=\,0.830; evaluated on the 5-generator subset for which cross-model chains were available), though these generators represent a controlled laboratory setting rather than the full diversity of real-world contamination.
Simulated human editing (\S\ref{sec:discussion}) suggests graceful degradation, but the gap between simulated token replacement and real-world post-processing remains untested.
Independent gen-0 seed sets per generator would eliminate potential memorization effects in 3-class LOGO evaluation; we report leak-free binary F1 as the primary metric to mitigate this limitation.

The reference model is fixed to Pythia-410M throughout, although cross-family reference experiments (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) confirm the phenomenon is not reference-specific (spread 0.013 across three references).
All seed texts in the main evaluation are English Wikipedia excerpts.
Cross-domain evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:domain}) shows that depth signal persists across News, Academic, and Code domains (binary F1 $>$ 0.73 under LOGO at $t{=}1.0$), though a domain $\times$ temperature interaction exists: certain domain/generator combinations at lower temperature approach chance level (e.g., Academic domain binary F1\,=\,0.628 at $t{=}0.7$), suggesting that reference model calibration is critical for cross-domain deployment.
The reference model dependency (Pythia-410M, English-centric pretraining) limits non-English applicability and adds inference overhead relative to surface-feature-only approaches.
Generalization to other languages remains untested.

Our default analysis uses fixed decoding parameters (temperature 0.7, nucleus $p{=}0.9$). A sampling ablation (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}) shows robustness to moderate variation ($t \in [0.5, 0.7]$, ${\leq}0.3$\,pp) but substantial degradation at $t{=}1.0$ ($-6$\,pp), indicating that depth fingerprinting assumes standard decoding regimes.
Cross-temperature transfer shows substantial degradation when test-time temperature exceeds training-time settings, limiting deployment to scenarios where the generation temperature is approximately known.

We use 3-class granularity (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+). A 5-class evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}) yields LOGO F1\,$\approx$\,0.50, with depths 2--4 mutually indistinguishable, validating the 3-class design as the practical resolution limit.

1	To assess whether depth signal extends beyond handcrafted features, we fine-tune a pretrained language model end-to-end as a depth classifier using QLoRA \cite{qlora}.
2	
3	\paragraph{Setup.}
4	We fine-tune Qwen3-0.6B-Base with LoRA rank 16, learning rate $2 \times 10^{-4}$, and 3 epochs, framing depth estimation as 5-class sequence classification (gen-0 through gen-4).\footnote{Evaluated on the original 6-generator subset; XGBoost 3-class F1\,=\,0.789. We expect 8-generator training to further improve given additional diversity; the comparison direction is preserved.}
5	For 3-class evaluation, we collapse predictions into gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+ post hoc.
6	All results use the same LOGO protocol as the main experiments.
7	
8	\begin{table}[ht]
9	\centering
10	\small
11	\caption{QLoRA end-to-end depth classification vs.\ XGBoost on handcrafted features, under LOGO evaluation.}
12	\label{tab:qlora}
13	\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
14	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
15	\toprule
16	\textbf{Method} & \textbf{5-class F1} & \textbf{3-class F1} & \textbf{Per-class F1 (5-class)} \\
17	\midrule
18	XGBoost (7 features) & 0.501 $\pm$ 0.038 & 0.789 & --- \\
19	QLoRA (Qwen3-0.6B)   & 0.583 $\pm$ 0.010 & 0.905 $\pm$ 0.003 & 0.999\,/\,0.796\,/\,0.413\,/\,0.259\,/\,0.447 \\
20	\bottomrule
21	\end{tabular}}
22	\end{table}
23	
24	\paragraph{Results.}
25	QLoRA achieves 3-class LOGO F1\,=\,0.905 ($\pm$0.003), a +11.6\,pp improvement over the XGBoost baseline (0.789).
26	On 5-class evaluation, QLoRA reaches F1\,=\,0.583 ($\pm$0.010) vs.\ 0.501 for XGBoost (+8.2\,pp), with the largest gains at gen-1 (0.796 vs.\ 0.634) and gen-2 (0.413 vs.\ 0.268).
27	The gen-2/gen-3 boundary remains the primary failure mode (gen-3 F1\,=\,0.259), consistent with the feature-level analysis in \S\ref{sec:discussion}.
28	
29	\paragraph{Hyperparameter robustness.}
30	A second run with LoRA rank 32 and seed 123 yields 5-class F1\,=\,0.587 ($\pm$0.005) and 3-class F1\,=\,0.905 ($\pm$0.004), which confirms stability across hyperparameter and seed variation ($\Delta < 1$\,pp on both metrics).
31	
32	\paragraph{Implications.}
33	The substantial 3-class improvement demonstrates that raw token embeddings contain depth signal beyond what summary statistics capture; the seven handcrafted features are a strong but lossy compression of the full distributional information.
34	End-to-end fine-tuning exploits token-level patterns (e.g., positional regularities, n-gram repetitions) that aggregate features cannot represent.
35	This confirms that the depth signal documented in our main analysis is real and exploitable beyond engineered features, while the handcrafted approach retains practical advantages: interpretability, computational efficiency (no GPU inference), and the ability to reveal the differential depth response pattern that motivates the task formulation.
36

1	We analyze the distribution and characteristics of binary classification errors (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) across the 8-generator LOGO evaluation ($N$\,=\,29{,}095 samples, overall error rate 28.08\%).
2	
3	\paragraph{Error asymmetry.}
4	Errors are heavily asymmetric: 86.2\% are false negatives (gen-2+ predicted as gen-1) and only 13.8\% are false positives (gen-1 predicted as gen-2+).
5	The classifier systematically under-predicts depth, consistent with the DDR pattern: shallow gen-2+ samples that have not yet accumulated sufficient distributional drift are indistinguishable from gen-1.
6	
7	\paragraph{Per-depth error rates.}
8	Error rates decrease monotonically with depth: depth-2 samples are the primary failure point (48.42\% error rate), followed by depth-3 (29.17\%) and depth-4 (20.32\%).
9	Depth-1 false positive rate is 7.11\%.
10	The monotonic decrease confirms that deeper generations accumulate progressively stronger depth signatures; the gen-1$\to$gen-2 transition is therefore the hardest to detect.
11	
12	\paragraph{Per-generator variation.}
13	Table~\ref{tab:error-by-gen} shows error rates vary substantially across generators, correlating with model scale: larger models (Mistral-7B, Qwen3-8B) produce text closer to gen-1 characteristics, which makes depth discrimination harder.
14	
15	\begin{table}[ht]
16	\centering
17	\small
18	\caption{Binary classification error rates by generator (8-gen LOGO). Sorted by error rate descending.}
19	\label{tab:error-by-gen}
20	\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
21	\begin{tabular}{llccc}
22	\toprule
23	\textbf{Generator} & \textbf{Family} & \textbf{Samples} & \textbf{Errors} & \textbf{Error rate} \\
24	\midrule
25	Mistral-7B-v0.3 & Mistral & 3{,}853 & 1{,}734 & 45.00\% \\
26	Qwen3-8B        & Qwen    & 3{,}502 & 1{,}197 & 34.18\% \\
27	Llama-3.2-3B    & Llama   & 3{,}685 & 1{,}112 & 30.18\% \\
28	OLMo-2-1B      & OLMo    & 3{,}718 & 1{,}054 & 28.35\% \\
29	Pythia-2.8B     & Pythia  & 3{,}614 &   866 & 23.96\% \\
30	Qwen3-1.7B     & Qwen    & 3{,}621 &   814 & 22.48\% \\
31	Qwen3-0.6B     & Qwen    & 3{,}542 &   745 & 21.03\% \\
32	Pythia-1B       & Pythia  & 3{,}560 &   648 & 18.20\% \\
33	\bottomrule
34	\end{tabular}}
35	\end{table}
36	
37	\paragraph{Feature-level explanation.}
38	Mann-Whitney U tests comparing correctly vs.\ incorrectly classified samples reveal that drifting features show significant distributional differences between correct and incorrect predictions: entropy\_mean ($p < 10^{-300}$), TTR ($p < 10^{-300}$), and hapax\_ratio ($p < 10^{-300}$).

We analyze the distribution and characteristics of binary classification errors (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) across the 8-generator LOGO evaluation ($N$\,=\,29{,}095 samples, overall error rate 28.08\%).

\paragraph{Error asymmetry.}
Errors are heavily asymmetric: 86.2\% are false negatives (gen-2+ predicted as gen-1) and only 13.8\% are false positives (gen-1 predicted as gen-2+).
The classifier systematically under-predicts depth, consistent with the DDR pattern: shallow gen-2+ samples that have not yet accumulated sufficient distributional drift are indistinguishable from gen-1.

\paragraph{Per-depth error rates.}
Error rates decrease monotonically with depth: depth-2 samples are the primary failure point (48.42\% error rate), followed by depth-3 (29.17\%) and depth-4 (20.32\%).
Depth-1 false positive rate is 7.11\%.
The monotonic decrease confirms that deeper generations accumulate progressively stronger depth signatures; the gen-1$\to$gen-2 transition is therefore the hardest to detect.

\paragraph{Per-generator variation.}
Table~\ref{tab:error-by-gen} shows error rates vary substantially across generators, correlating with model scale: larger models (Mistral-7B, Qwen3-8B) produce text closer to gen-1 characteristics, which makes depth discrimination harder.

\textbf{Generator} & \textbf{Family} & \textbf{Samples} & \textbf{Errors} & \textbf{Error rate} \\

Pythia-1B       & Pythia  & 3{,}560 &   648 & 18.20\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}

\paragraph{Feature-level explanation.}
Mann-Whitney U tests comparing correctly vs.\ incorrectly classified samples reveal that drifting features show significant distributional differences between correct and incorrect predictions: entropy\_mean ($p < 10^{-300}$), TTR ($p < 10^{-300}$), and hapax\_ratio ($p < 10^{-300}$).
In contrast, shape features show no discriminating power: entropy\_max ($p = 0.584$) and tail\_decay ($p = 0.653$).
Misclassified gen-2+ samples have systematically higher TTR (0.464 vs.\ 0.302 for correct) and entropy\_mean (2.26 vs.\ 1.57); these samples retain gen-1-like lexical diversity and have not undergone the distributional convergence characteristic of deeper generations.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

AI text detection asks a single binary question---\emph{human or machine?}---and recent methods answer it with increasing reliability \cite{detectgpt,fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score}.
Yet this framing elides a richer structure emerging on the open web: as LLM outputs re-enter training corpora \cite{dolma,fineweb} and seed further generation, text accumulates at varying \emph{recursive depths}---an estimated 7--17\% of recent scientific publications already contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}---and each generation cycle pushes distributional properties further from both the human source and the first-generation predecessor.
Knowing \emph{how many times} text has been recursively generated matters for data provenance \cite{ccnet,dsir} and model collapse analysis \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse}, yet no current method moves beyond the binary boundary.

We introduce \emph{depth fingerprinting}: classifying text by ordinal generation depth (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) and decomposing the distributional drift that accumulates across depths into structurally distinct components.
The core empirical finding is a \emph{differential depth response} (DDR): across eight base-model generators spanning five architectural families (0.6B--8B), the NLL distribution's central tendency (mean entropy, lexical diversity) drifts monotonically with depth while its shape (entropy extremes, tail structure) remains an order of magnitude more stable ($d{=}0.76$--$1.17$ vs.\ $d < 0.10$; five independent effect-size metrics converge on this partition).
This location/shape asymmetry exposes a structural property of fixed-parameter autoregressive sampling: the decoding mechanism systematically compresses where the output distribution sits while preserving its higher-order form---a pattern mechanistically distinct from the tail-coverage erosion in model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion}, and analytically informative independent of classification accuracy.
Concurrent work characterizes convergence in paraphrastic and translation chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains}; ours is the first to decompose the drift into complementary location and shape components and to leverage this asymmetry for cross-generator depth prediction.
We restrict to base (pretrained) models to isolate the generation dynamics from alignment artifacts (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

As a proof of concept, a lightweight 7-feature ensemble informed by DDR achieves leak-free binary F1\,=\,0.694 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation, surpassing individual detection baselines by 6.7--36.3\,pp; an end-to-end QLoRA classifier reaches 0.905, confirming that the depth signal extends well beyond handcrafted features.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Empirical decomposition (DDR).} Data-driven clustering ($k{=}2$, silhouette\,=\,0.632) reveals that inference-chain drift separates into a drifting location component ($d{=}0.76$--$1.17$) and a stable shape component ($d < 0.10$). Where prior work documents \emph{what converges}, DDR identifies \emph{what is preserved}---enabling depth detection without per-generator calibration.
    \item \textbf{Task formulation and evaluation suite.} We define generation depth classification as an ordinal prediction task and construct a controlled dataset of 37K texts from eight generators across five families (0.6B--8B), with leave-one-generator-out cross-validation as the primary evaluation protocol.
\end{enumerate}
We additionally provide a proof-of-concept classifier (binary F1\,=\,0.694) and systematically map its operating boundaries across temperature, prompt type, instruction tuning, and model scale, establishing where DDR-based detection succeeds and where it fails.

5	\label{sec:results-classification}
6	
7	Before analyzing the DDR decomposition (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}), we establish that generation depth is classifiable across diverse architectures.
8	The 7-feature ensemble achieves 3-class LOGO F1\,=\,0.762 (95\% CI [0.758, 0.766]; $N$\,=\,37{,}058) across eight generators from five families (Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}).
9	Because gen-0 seeds are shared across generators (\S\ref{sec:generation}), gen-0 classification is near-perfect (per-class F1\,$\approx$\,0.94), inflating the 3-class metric.
10	We therefore adopt \textbf{leak-free binary F1} (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+)\,=\,0.694 (CI [0.688, 0.700]) as the primary metric throughout: it excludes gen-0 entirely and is unaffected by seed sharing.
11	Per-generator binary F1 ranges from 0.633 (Mistral-7B) to 0.724 (Pythia-2.8B), with the primary difficulty concentrated at the gen-1\,/\,gen-2+ boundary (Appendix~\ref{app:confusion}).

13	\paragraph{Cross-model generalization.}
14	Cross-model chains (randomly selected generator per step) yield binary F1\,=\,0.830 (95\% CI [.818, .841]) under 5-generator LOGO.\footnote{5-generator subset (Pythia-2.8B/1B, OLMo-2-1B, Qwen3-0.6B/1.7B); generator-level LOGO with bootstrap CIs ($n$\,=\,2{,}000). Not directly comparable to 8-generator LOGO due to differing subsets.}

56	\caption{Feature trajectories across generation depth. \textbf{Top row (drifting)}: entropy mean and hapax ratio decline monotonically across all eight generators ($|\rho| > 0.59$). \textbf{Bottom row (stationary)}: entropy max and tail decay remain flat ($|\rho| < 0.07$). 59	
60	Not all distributional properties respond equally to recursive generation.
61	Figure~\ref{fig:ddr-trajectory} reveals a striking dichotomy that holds across all eight generators: central-tendency features (entropy mean, TTR, hapax ratio) decline monotonically with depth, while shape features (entropy max, tail decay, entropy min) remain flat.
62	We term this asymmetry the \emph{differential depth response} (DDR).
63	The primary partition is binary: $k{=}2$ clustering in standardized $(|\rho|, d)$ space yields silhouette\,=\,0.632 (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}), cleanly separating three \emph{drifting} features ($|\rho| > 0.60$, $d{=}0.76$--$1.17$) from four \emph{non-drifting} ones ($d \leq 0.55$); higher $k$ degrades cluster quality ($k{=}3$: silhouette\,=\,0.499).

Entropy min ($|\rho|{=}0.40$ pooled) is a boundary feature whose sensitivity concentrates at the gen-0/gen-1 transition.}

75	drifting features show substantial monotonic trends (hapax ratio $\rho = -0.64$, TTR $\rho = -0.63$, entropy mean $\rho = -0.60$),
76	while non-drifting features remain near-zero (tail decay $|\rho| = 0.04$; per-depth distributions in Appendix~\ref{app:feature-distributions}).
77	The six-fold magnitude gap between drifting ($|\rho| > 0.60$) and non-drifting features ($|\rho| \leq 0.16$) defines the DDR partition.
78	Within the non-drifting group, entropy std ($|\rho| = 0.16$, $d{=}0.55$) shows a substantial level shift despite low monotonicity, distinguishing it from the three near-stationary features ($d < 0.10$); this refinement is stable across $d$ thresholds in $[0.56, 0.75]$ (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}).
79	
80	\paragraph{Quantification.}
81	Every tested effect-size metric confirms the split.
82	Cohen's $d$ \cite{cohen1988statistical} converges with $\rho$: drifting features show large effects ($d{=}0.76$--$1.17$) while shape features are near zero ($d \leq 0.08$); KS statistics show a ${\sim}10\times$ gap (0.516--0.537 vs.\ 0.043--0.052; all $p \approx 0$).
83	Glass's $\Delta$ and Cliff's $\delta$ corroborate the partition with a ${\geq}9.5\times$ gap; CV shift ($<$3\% vs.\ $>$15\%) supports ``near-stationary'' as a practical characterization (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}).
84	Five features fall cleanly into drifting or non-drifting groups; the remaining two require qualification.
85	Entropy min is a \emph{boundary feature}: its gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ effect is near-stationary ($d{=}0.016$) despite a substantial pooled $|\rho|$ (0.40) driven by the gen-0/gen-1 transition (Cliff's $\delta{=}0.354$ confirms shape change without location shift); $k{=}2$ clustering places it with non-drifting features (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}).
86	Entropy std shows a substantial level shift ($d{=}0.55$) despite low monotonicity ($|\rho|{=}0.16$), making it the sole intermediate feature.
87	\paragraph{Validation.}
88	The partition is not a pooling artifact.
89	Per-generator TOST equivalence testing ($\varepsilon{=}|d|{<}0.20$, gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) confirms stability for entropy min (8/8 generators pass) and entropy max (6/8); tail decay passes for only 4/8 generators, with OLMo-2-1B ($d{=}0.22$) exceeding the equivalence bound (Appendix~\ref{app:tost}).
90	Bootstrap resampling (1{,}000 iterations) on the pooled sample achieves 100\% rejection for all three near-stationary features, but high pooled power ($N \approx 3{,}500$--$4{,}500$ per generator) can mask per-generator heterogeneity.
91	Tail decay's 50\% per-generator pass rate represents a genuine boundary case: reclassifying it as intermediate preserves the core drifting/non-drifting split and classification performance (F1 change $<$0.5\,pp).
92	
93	\paragraph{Feature complementarity.}
94	The full 7-feature set (F1\,=\,0.773) outperforms surface-only (0.688) and reference-only (0.713; McNemar $p \approx 0$; Appendix~\ref{app:ablation-table}).

96	TTR and hapax ratio ($r = 0.97$) are both retained for marginal LOFO gains despite feature masking \cite{strobl_conditional_2008} (Appendix~\ref{app:lofo}).
